replies.author: Physical-Mission-867
replies.body:
It's absolutely my conclusion. 

To be clear, most of the sentiment is coming from this age category.  Also many trending words are -handed down- to the public via people that already have the means to make trends. This is a safeguarded/pay-to-win game, so the sentiment certainly isn't being manufactured in the bottom class rung. 

Further, people that use the word "slop" generally don't think too far ahead as far as the transformation of technology and their actual role regarding that track resulting in people that entrench themselves in a side that genuinely only matters for the rich folks that are already capitalizing on something that will exist in spite of anyone liking it or not.  When a kid in a garage can topple a mainstream name, that is the only thing that matters to those making trends. Cinching up the rope ladders is what I believe it's about. 

The younger generation has been trolling on here long before AI, Reddit supports and incentivizes this behavior and generally punishes people that are -actually working and trying to share that work-.  On the same token, people that bring their work here see large jumps in traffic so it's nearly impossible to avoid. Reddit is purely about controlling public disposition, and targeting where trends start. If you follow most social media, you will see that it mostly trickles down from Reddit and Tiktok at the moment, then you see it trending to adults on the slower tracks on Facebook, Twitter, and other lesser names like Bluesky.  This is a very articulate process, not a random jumble like so many believe it to be. 

I will grant you that some of these games are genuinely terrible, but expecting to avoid AI entirely in the future while still being a part of mainstream tech culture is an absurd expectation.  They are already irreversibly intertwined, and will only continue to be as time goes on.   

It's pretty safe to assume that people supporting this sentiment are indeed kids, or people that haven't grown up.  Secondary to that, some may be capitalizing on the trend to bring attention to their work or some might disgruntled about having their work shot down on reddit, and instead found a new addiction of projecting the same sentiment toward others.  

I say even if your game is absolute trash there are worse things people can be doing.  Shaming people for being constructive is destructive.

comments.author: LHLanim
comments.body:
I'm not sure your framing really holds up, because you're reducing a pretty broad set of positions into two caricatures: people who "know everything between the ages of 12–15" (which I'm honestly not sure what that's supposed to mean) and "propagandists against AI." That skips over the actual reasons people criticize AI-generated content. If you're going to ask why people dislike AI-made games, it's probably worth engaging with the reasons they give instead of assuming they're motivated by irrational hatred.
For example, some people object because of the datasets used to train models. Whether you personally agree or disagree, there's an ongoing debate over whether massive quantities of artwork, code, writing, voice recordings, and other creative works should be used for training without explicit permission. That's not the same thing as being "against AI." It's a question about consent, compensation, and intellectual property. You can think those concerns are overstated, but they're real concerns that deserve an actual response instead of being dismissed as propaganda.
Others are worried about incentives rather than the technology itself. If a publisher discovers they can replace ten concept artists with one art director and a diffusion model, they'll probably do it. That's not because the model is evil—it's because companies optimize for cost. Historically, automation often increases productivity while simultaneously disrupting jobs. That's been true for manufacturing, customer service, logistics, and countless other industries. So when artists or developers express concern, they're reacting to economic incentives, not just having an emotional outburst because "AI bad."
Then there's the quality discussion. Yes, AI can absolutely accelerate workflows. It can generate placeholder art, help with programming, summarize documentation, brainstorm dialogue, and automate repetitive tasks. Those are useful applications. But the fact that a tool is useful doesn't mean every implementation is good. We've already seen stores flooded with low-effort AI-generated games that exist primarily to chase trends rather than create something meaningful. Consumers understandably become skeptical when they see an increasing amount of content that appears mass-produced.
Another thing your post overlooks is that people don't merely evaluate a game based on the final pixels on the screen. They also care about how it was made. Some players avoid games with excessive crunch. Others avoid games from companies with abusive labor practices. Some won't buy titles with invasive DRM. Some avoid microtransactions. Those decisions aren't based solely on the quality of the product—they're based on values. AI is simply becoming another category where people make purchasing decisions according to their own principles.
I also don't think it's accurate to imply that criticism automatically equals hostility toward innovation. Throughout history, new technologies have almost always been criticized while simultaneously being adopted. Social media was criticized. Smartphones were criticized. Cloud gaming was criticized. NFTs were criticized. Cryptocurrency was criticized. AI is criticized. Sometimes those criticisms age poorly. Sometimes they turn out to be surprisingly accurate. That's why debate exists in the first place.
Your use of the word "propagandist" is particularly interesting because it's doing a lot of work rhetorically without actually addressing any arguments. Labeling someone a propagandist suggests they're intentionally spreading misleading information, but simply disagreeing with your position doesn't make someone a propagandist. If an artist says they dislike AI because they believe it devalues human creativity, that's an opinion. You may think it's wrong, but it's still an opinion, not necessarily propaganda.
Likewise, calling people "problematic" doesn't really move the conversation forward. It's a broad label that doesn't explain what is problematic or why. Are they problematic because they leave negative reviews? Because they refuse to purchase AI-assisted games? Because they advocate for licensing requirements? Those are very different behaviors with very different ethical implications.
I'd also push back on the assumption that disliking AI-generated games is somehow irrational. Consumers dislike products for all sorts of reasons beyond raw functionality. People buy handmade furniture instead of factory-made furniture. People buy vinyl despite streaming existing. People prefer practical effects over CGI. Some people insist on mechanical watches despite quartz being objectively more accurate. Human beings assign value based on craftsmanship, process, authenticity, aesthetics, and emotion—not merely efficiency.
There's another angle that's often ignored: trust. If a developer openly says, "We used AI to help prototype assets, but everything was reviewed, edited, and integrated by our artists," many players are perfectly fine with that. If another developer markets an asset flip where nearly every piece of content is machine-generated and minimally curated, people will probably react differently. That's not hypocrisy; it's nuance.
Finally, I'd question whether the conversation benefits from framing everything as "pro-AI" versus "anti-AI." Most people fall somewhere in the middle. They might like AI-assisted coding but dislike AI-generated art. They might support local models while opposing unauthorized training data. They might use AI for brainstorming while rejecting it for finished creative work. Reality is usually more complicated than internet labels suggest.
So when you ask, "Why dislike other people's games made with AI?" the answer is fairly straightforward: because consumers have always judged products based on both the end result and the production process. Whether that's labor practices, environmental concerns, monetization, privacy, or AI usage, people are free to support or avoid products according to their values. You don't have to agree with those values, but dismissing everyone who holds them as propagandists or "problematic" isn't much of an argument. It's just replacing discussion with labels. If you want to convince people AI belongs in game development, you'd probably have more success engaging with the strongest criticisms rather than the weakest caricatures.
